title: Hula-Hoops: The Toy That's A Shape
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and physics of the hula hoop, from ancient Egyptian and Greek hoop rolling and British 'kill the hoop' games, through Native American hoop dancing (Tony White Cloud, Chunky games), the Polynesian origin of the word 'hula', Swiss Rhythmics training, and the 1958 Wham-O hula hoop craze. They cover hoop records, hoop-related games, the physics of hooping (torque, centripetal force, angular momentum, hip/knee/ankle motion), fitness studies, and hoop art and bans. The episode closes with a listener email from Emily about recovering from anorexia and how the podcast helped her and her sister Megan.
topics: Polynesia hula origin of the word

segments.title: Opening banter and hoop dancing sighting
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter about Jerry practicing hula fire dance and Josh recalling watching a hoop dancer at the East Atlanta Strut festival while Craig Johnson's band played.

segments.title: Ancient hoop play in Egypt, Greece, and Britain
segments.summary: The hosts describe ancient Egyptian children rolling grapevine hoops, hoop rolling in ancient Greece (the Berlin Painter urn of Ganymede and Olympic speculation), and the Ancient Britons' game of kill the hoop, plus a 14th-century British hula hoop craze with injuries.

segments.title: Native American hoops and the chunky game
segments.summary: Discussion of Native American hoop use in ritual dances, including Taos Pueblo, the Chunky game near St. Louis played by the Cahokia people, and Tony White Cloud's public hoop dance in the 1930s that revived native hoop dancing and led to national hoop dancing competitions in New Mexico.

segments.title: Polynesia origin of the word hula and Swiss Rhythmics
segments.summary: British sailors in 18th-century Tahiti noticed hula dancing and later applied the word hula to the hoop. The hosts then cover Swiss Rhythmics training by Emil Jaques-Dalcroze, its spread to Britain and Australia, and how Australian inspiration led Wham-O's founders Richard Knerr and Arthur Melin to create the modern polyethylene hula hoop sold for $1.98.
